evidence: src/domain/value-objects/DueDate.ts: private constructor plus static fromIsoString(raw) that throws ValidationError when the date doesn't parse

src/domain/value-objects/TaskStatus.ts: private constructor plus static from(raw) that throws ValidationError and uses TASK_STATUSES as the single list of statuses for the error message and the TaskStatusValue type
src/domain/value-objects/TaskTitle.ts: private constructor plus static create(raw) that enforces non-empty and TaskTitle.MAX_LENGTH, throwing ValidationError
All three files import only ValidationError from ../errors/DomainError, so they report errors the same way

Minor, within one file: TaskStatus.ts writes the status strings out in TASK_STATUSES, in the static instances and in the from() switch, and isDone() compares against the string 'done' instead of TaskStatus.DONE
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The three files form one cohesive concern: a validated, immutable value object for each task attribute (due date, status, title). All three share one pattern: a private constructor, a static factory that validates raw input, and the shared ValidationError from ../errors/DomainError on failure. Each rule lives in one place. The title length limit is TaskTitle.MAX_LENGTH, the allowed statuses are TASK_STATUSES/TaskStatusValue in TaskStatus.ts, and date parsing is DueDate.fromIsoString. No file bypasses another's factory. Smaller issues: inside TaskStatus.ts the status strings appear in TASK_STATUSES, in the static instances and in the switch in from(), and isDone() compares against the string 'done' instead of TaskStatus.DONE. Since from() switches on a plain string, the compiler won't catch a missed spot when a status is added. DueDate has no equals() and doesn't expose its value the way the other two do. Both are small, contained inside single files, and don't amount to a split concern or a rule duplicated across files.
